questions.question: What does neurogenesis refer to?
options: Expansion of neural tissue without producing new cells
Generation of neurons from neural progenitor cells
Migration of mature neurons to their final targets
Selective elimination of newly generated neurons
questions.feedback: The lesson defines neurogenesis as the generation of neurons from neural progenitor cells.

questions.question: What is the main difference between progenitor proliferation and neurogenesis?
options: Proliferation expands the progenitor pool, whereas neurogenesis produces neurons
Proliferation produces neurons, whereas neurogenesis produces only progenitors
Proliferation occurs only after migration
Neurogenesis does not involve cell division
questions.feedback: Proliferative divisions increase the number of progenitors, whereas neurogenic divisions generate cells that enter a neuronal developmental program.

questions.question: Which sequence best represents the developmental progression described in the lesson?
options: Migration → proliferation → apoptosis → differentiation
Progenitor proliferation → cell-cycle exit → migration → differentiation → survival or programmed cell death
Differentiation → proliferation → cell-cycle entry → migration
Programmed cell death → proliferation → migration → neurogenesis
questions.feedback: The lesson presents proliferation, cell-cycle exit, migration, differentiation, and survival or programmed cell death as a connected developmental sequence.

questions.question: Where are early cortical progenitors located?
options: In the cortical plate
Close to the cerebral ventricles in the ventricular zone
Only in the subplate
Outside the developing telencephalon
questions.feedback: Early cortical progenitors are concentrated near the cerebral ventricles in the ventricular zone.

questions.question: What are the two major developmental roles of radial glial cells emphasized in the lesson?
options: Producing myelin and eliminating synapses
Acting as neural progenitors and providing a scaffold for neuronal migration
Forming only inhibitory neurons and guiding axons
Generating blood vessels and synaptic targets
questions.feedback: Radial glial cells act as neural progenitors and their long processes provide a scaffold for neuronal migration.

questions.question: What is the outcome of a symmetric proliferative division?
options: Two neurons
One progenitor and one neuron
Two progenitor cells
One neuron and one glial cell
questions.feedback: A symmetric proliferative division produces two progenitor cells and therefore expands the progenitor population.

questions.question: What is a typical outcome of an asymmetric neurogenic division?
options: Two identical progenitors
One progenitor and one neuron
Two mature astrocytes
One apoptotic cell and one progenitor
questions.feedback: The lesson uses progenitor → progenitor + neuron as the example of an asymmetric neurogenic division.

questions.question: Why are intermediate progenitor cells important during cortical neurogenesis?
options: They stop all further cell division
They provide an additional amplification step for neuron production
They form only the ventricular lining
They prevent radial migration
questions.feedback: Intermediate progenitors divide away from the ventricular surface and provide an additional amplification step in neuron production.

questions.question: How do many excitatory cortical neurons reach their final positions?
options: They migrate along radial glial processes
They remain permanently in the ventricular zone
They migrate only along blood vessels
They are carried by neural crest cells
questions.feedback: Many excitatory cortical neurons migrate outward along the long processes of radial glial cells.

questions.question: What happens to newly generated cortical neurons after leaving proliferative zones?
options: They become postmitotic and migrate outward
They immediately return to the ventricular zone
They remain proliferative throughout migration
They become neural crest cells
questions.feedback: The lesson describes newly generated neurons as becoming postmitotic and migrating outward toward the cortical plate.

questions.question: What does the inside-out pattern of cortical development mean?
options: Later-born neurons remain in deep layers while early-born neurons move superficially
Earlier-born neurons occupy deeper layers and later-born neurons migrate past them to more superficial layers
All cortical layers are generated simultaneously
Only superficial neurons migrate
questions.feedback: In inside-out development, early-born neurons settle deeper, while later-born neurons migrate past them to progressively more superficial layers.

questions.question: What is strongly related to the laminar identity of cortical neurons?
options: The time of the progenitor's final mitosis
Only the final size of the neuron
The number of synapses formed in adulthood
Whether the neuron is exposed to blood flow
questions.feedback: The lesson emphasizes that neuronal birthdate, defined by the timing of the final mitosis, is strongly related to cortical identity.

questions.question: What question is tested by heterochronic transplantation of cortical progenitors?
options: Whether laminar identity is determined only by the environment in which a progenitor is placed
Whether neurons can survive without oxygen
Whether radial glia are generated from neural crest cells
Whether apoptosis occurs before neurogenesis
questions.feedback: Heterochronic transplantation tests whether progenitor fate is determined only by the new environment or also by the progenitor's developmental state.

questions.question: What does heterochronic transplantation show about cortical progenitors?
options: Their developmental potential remains unchanged at all ages
Their ability to adopt a new laminar fate depends on developmental age and cell-cycle state
They cannot respond to environmental information
Their fate is fixed before any cell division
questions.feedback: The lesson states that the capacity to adopt a new laminar fate depends on developmental age and cell-cycle state.

questions.question: How does progenitor competence change during cortical development?
options: It becomes progressively more restricted
It becomes progressively unlimited
It is unrelated to developmental time
It disappears before neurogenesis begins
questions.feedback: As progenitors progress through development, their possible fates become progressively restricted.

questions.question: What does neuronal differentiation involve?
options: Only an increase in cell number
Acquisition of morphology, transmitter phenotype, receptor expression, gene-expression patterns, and characteristic connectivity
Only migration from the ventricular zone
Only elimination of excess neurons
questions.feedback: Differentiation is presented as the acquisition of multiple features that define a specific neuronal identity.

questions.question: Which of the following is an intrinsic factor influencing neural cell fate?
options: A transcription factor already expressed by the cell
A secreted molecule from a neighboring tissue
An extracellular matrix signal
A target-derived trophic factor
questions.feedback: Transcription factors, inherited cellular components, developmental history, and competence are listed as intrinsic influences on fate.

questions.question: Which of the following is an extrinsic factor influencing neural cell fate?
options: Previous developmental history
Asymmetric inheritance of intracellular components
Signals from neighboring cells
The cell's existing transcription-factor profile
questions.feedback: Signals from neighboring cells are extrinsic because they originate outside the responding cell.

questions.question: What is the role of Delta in Notch-Delta lateral inhibition?
options: It activates Notch in neighboring cells
It directly activates caspases
It blocks all neuronal differentiation in the Delta-expressing cell
It acts only as an intracellular transcription factor
questions.feedback: In the lesson, stronger proneural/Delta activity in one cell activates Notch in neighboring cells.

questions.question: What effect does Notch activation have on the neuronal program in neighboring progenitor cells?
options: It enhances the neuronal program
It suppresses the neuronal program
It directly causes necrosis
It converts neurons into radial glia after migration
questions.feedback: Notch signaling suppresses the neuronal program in neighboring cells during lateral inhibition.

questions.question: What is lateral inhibition?
options: A mechanism that amplifies small differences between neighboring cells so they acquire different fates
A process that makes all neighboring cells adopt the same fate
A type of programmed cell death
A mechanism for radial migration
questions.feedback: Lateral inhibition amplifies small initial differences and allows initially similar neighboring cells to acquire different developmental fates.

questions.question: What role does Numb play in the lesson's example of asymmetric fate?
options: It can antagonize Notch signaling
It directly activates NGF receptors
It acts as a target-derived trophic factor
It forms the radial glial scaffold
questions.feedback: Numb is presented as a regulatory molecule that can antagonize Notch signaling.

questions.question: Why can asymmetric inheritance during cell division produce different daughter-cell fates?
options: The daughters can inherit different amounts of fate-regulating molecules
The daughters always receive different genomes
Only one daughter remains alive
One daughter necessarily leaves the nervous system
questions.feedback: Unequal inheritance of regulatory molecules can cause daughter cells from the same progenitor to respond differently and follow different developmental trajectories.

questions.question: What developmental role is associated with Dlx1/Dlx2 in the lesson?
options: Development and migration of forebrain interneurons
Formation of the ventricular lumen
Activation of the apoptotic caspase cascade
Production of target-derived trophic factors
questions.feedback: Dlx1/Dlx2 are presented as transcription factors involved in forebrain interneuron development, with disruption strongly affecting migration toward the neocortex.

questions.question: What does the Dlx1/Dlx2 example demonstrate more generally?
options: Gene expression can influence cell identity, migration, and final regional organization
Migration is independent of transcription factors
Only extracellular matrix determines neuronal identity
All interneurons are generated in the cortical plate
questions.feedback: The lesson uses Dlx1/Dlx2 to show that intrinsic gene-expression programs can affect identity, migration, and regional organization.

questions.question: Why can migration influence the fate of a developing neural cell?
options: Migrating cells encounter new extracellular environments and signals
Migration removes all receptors from the cell
Migrating cells stop responding to neighboring tissues
Migration fixes cell fate before any environmental interaction
questions.feedback: As cells migrate, they encounter different signaling molecules, neighboring cells, extracellular matrix components, and target tissues that can provide new developmental instructions.

questions.question: Why are neural crest cells used as an example of environmental control of fate?
options: They are multipotent progenitors whose fate depends strongly on signals encountered during migration
They generate only one neuronal subtype
They never migrate
Their fate is independent of extracellular signals
questions.feedback: Neural crest cells are multipotent and can generate diverse derivatives depending strongly on the signals they encounter during migration.

questions.question: Which combination best captures the lesson's model of cell fate?
options: Intrinsic state + extracellular signals + developmental time + competence
Cell size + blood flow + synapse number + age
Migration + apoptosis only
Gene expression alone
questions.feedback: The lesson summarizes cell fate as an interaction among intrinsic state, extracellular signals, developmental time, and competence.

questions.question: Why can the same extracellular signal produce different outcomes in different cells?
options: Cells can differ in developmental history, receptors, and gene-regulatory programs
Extracellular signals are always random
All cells interpret the same signal identically
Only cell size determines the response
questions.feedback: The lesson explains that different histories, receptor expression, and gene-regulatory programs change how a cell interprets the same signal.

questions.question: What is a central feature of neuronal survival during development?
options: Every neuron generated by neurogenesis is retained
Many neuronal populations initially produce more neurons than will ultimately survive
Neuronal survival is determined before neurogenesis
Only glial cells undergo developmental selection
questions.feedback: The lesson emphasizes that many developing neuronal populations are initially overproduced and then undergo selective survival.

questions.question: How is programmed cell death presented in the lesson?
options: As a normal component of nervous system development
As evidence that development has failed
As a process restricted to disease
As identical to necrosis
questions.feedback: Programmed cell death is described as a normal and active component of nervous system development.

questions.question: Which of the following is classified as a regressive developmental process?
options: Progenitor expansion
Neurogenesis
Programmed neuronal death
Neuronal growth
questions.feedback: Programmed neuronal death is listed among regressive processes, whereas progenitor expansion, neurogenesis, and growth are constructive processes.

questions.question: Which feature is characteristic of apoptosis?
options: Cell shrinkage and chromatin condensation
Cell swelling and membrane rupture
Release of intracellular contents with strong inflammation
Uncontrolled tissue injury
questions.feedback: Apoptosis is characterized by cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, fragmentation into apoptotic bodies, and little inflammatory response.

questions.question: Which feature is characteristic of necrosis?
options: Cell swelling and membrane disruption
Formation of apoptotic bodies with little inflammation
A tightly regulated developmental program
Selective survival after target competition
questions.feedback: Necrosis is described as involving cell swelling, membrane disruption, release of intracellular contents, and inflammation.

questions.question: What role is attributed to BCL-2 family proteins in the apoptosis slide?
options: Some members promote cell survival
They are all caspases
They are extracellular target-derived factors
They generate radial glial cells
questions.feedback: BCL-2 family proteins are presented as important regulators, with some members promoting survival.

questions.question: What role is attributed to BAX and related proteins?
options: They promote apoptosis
They inhibit all cell death
They provide a scaffold for migration
They act as neurotrophic targets
questions.feedback: BAX and related proteins are presented as pro-apoptotic regulators.

questions.question: What is the role of caspases in programmed cell death?
options: They execute the cell-death program
They expand the progenitor pool
They guide radial migration
They determine cortical layer birthdate
questions.feedback: The lesson identifies caspases as executors of the apoptotic cell-death program.

questions.question: Why can programmed neuronal death be useful during development?
options: It can match interconnected populations and remove inappropriate or transient cells
It prevents any refinement of neural structures
It ensures every generated neuron survives
It replaces neurogenesis
questions.feedback: Programmed cell death can match population sizes, remove inappropriate identities or connections, eliminate transient cells, and refine developing structures.

questions.question: What happens to developing neurons that successfully interact with appropriate target tissues?
options: They receive survival signals
They necessarily undergo necrosis
They return to the ventricular zone
They lose their differentiated identity
questions.feedback: The lesson states that successful interaction with appropriate targets provides survival signals to developing neurons.

questions.question: What did the experiments of Viktor Hamburger and Rita Levi-Montalcini demonstrate?
options: Peripheral target tissues influence the survival of developing neurons
Cortical layers form from superficial to deep
Notch directly activates neuronal differentiation
Neural crest cells never change fate
questions.feedback: Their chick-embryo experiments showed that manipulating peripheral target tissue changes the number of developing neurons that survive.

questions.question: What is the effect of removing developing target tissue in the Hamburger-Levi-Montalcini paradigm?
options: Increased neuronal loss
Increased neuronal survival
No change in neuronal survival
Conversion of motor neurons into progenitors
questions.feedback: Removing target tissue increases neuronal loss because fewer target-derived survival resources are available.

questions.question: What is the effect of adding extra target tissue in the target-manipulation experiment?
options: Increased neuronal survival
Complete elimination of the neuronal population
Suppression of neurogenesis
Loss of all radial glial cells
questions.feedback: Adding extra target tissue increases neuronal survival by increasing the available target support.

questions.question: What does the classical neurotrophic hypothesis propose?
options: Developing neurons compete for a limited amount of target-derived survival factors
Every neuron receives unlimited trophic support
Target tissues determine only neuronal migration, not survival
Apoptosis is independent of extracellular signals
questions.feedback: The classical neurotrophic hypothesis proposes competition among developing neurons for limited target-derived survival factors.

questions.question: According to the neurotrophic hypothesis, which neurons are most likely to survive?
options: Those that obtain sufficient trophic support from their targets
Those that never contact a target
Those that remain permanently proliferative
Those that activate the apoptotic program first
questions.feedback: Neurons obtaining sufficient target-derived trophic support survive, whereas those receiving insufficient support undergo apoptosis.

questions.question: What is the role of NGF emphasized in the lesson?
options: It supports the development and survival of particular peripheral sensory and sympathetic neuronal populations
It is a universal survival factor for every neuron
It is an intracellular caspase
It determines the inside-out sequence of cortical layers
questions.feedback: NGF is described as essential for particular peripheral sensory and sympathetic neuronal populations, but not as a universal survival factor.

questions.question: What does the lesson emphasize about neurotrophic factors beyond NGF?
options: Different neuronal populations can depend on different neurotrophic factors
All neurons depend exclusively on NGF
Neurotrophic factors act only during migration
Neurotrophic factors are produced only by progenitor cells
questions.feedback: The lesson emphasizes that different neuronal populations depend on different members of the broader neurotrophic-factor family.

questions.question: How does reducing target size affect neurotrophic competition?
options: It reduces trophic support, increases competition, and increases neuronal death
It increases trophic support and reduces neuronal death
It eliminates competition without affecting survival
It causes all neurons to become progenitors
questions.feedback: A smaller target provides less trophic support, creating stronger competition and more neuronal death.

questions.question: How does enlarging the target affect neuronal survival in the lesson's model?
options: More trophic support weakens competition and increases survival
More trophic support strengthens competition and increases death
Target size has no relation to survival
A larger target prevents neuronal differentiation
questions.feedback: A larger or additional target provides more trophic support, reducing competition and allowing more neurons to survive.

questions.question: How do target-derived trophic factors influence the intrinsic apoptotic machinery?
options: They activate intracellular pathways that can inhibit or permit the cell-death program
They act only as nutrients and do not affect signaling
They always activate apoptosis
They influence only progenitor proliferation
questions.feedback: The lesson emphasizes that trophic factors activate receptors and intracellular pathways that regulate the balance between survival and apoptosis.

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes the overall developmental principle of the lesson?
options: The mature nervous system emerges through generation, selection, and refinement
Development consists only of producing as many neurons as possible
Cell elimination is always pathological
Once neurons are generated, their identity and survival are fixed
questions.feedback: The lesson concludes that the mature nervous system is produced through repeated cycles of generation, selection, and refinement.
